column3: The Hebrew has both “spoke” and “saying”; BSB condenses these to “said.”
The Hebrew gives both “speak” and “say to them”; BSB gives a single “Say.”
The Hebrew repeats “his flesh” in the flowing and blocked descriptions; BSB gives “his body” once and then uses “it.”
The Hebrew names the man’s “flesh”; BSB uses “body.”
The Hebrew says to wash “his flesh” in “living water”; BSB says to bathe “himself” in “fresh water.”
The Hebrew calls the young pigeons “sons of a dove”; BSB says “young pigeons.”
The Hebrew says to wash “all his flesh”; BSB says to bathe “his whole body.”
The Hebrew gives lying and sitting separate clauses, repeating “shall be unclean”; BSB joins the actions with “or” under a single uncleanness clause.
The Hebrew emphasizes lying with a repeated verb and says her menstrual impurity “is on him”; BSB gives the lying verb once and specifies that the menstrual flow “touches him.”
The Hebrew separately compares the bed to her menstrual bed and the furniture to her menstrual uncleanness; BSB joins bed and furniture under one comparison to her bed.
The Hebrew says she will be “clean,” without an explicit word “ceremonially”; BSB adds that qualifier.
The Hebrew calls the young pigeons “sons of a dove”; BSB says “young pigeons.”
